opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few layers to it.

The first is fairly practical: talent and ecosystem. If you're a large internet company, your core competitive advantage usually isn't one piece of infrastructure software. It's your product, your users, your data, and how fast you can iterate. A deep learning framework or a distributed systems tool is very important, but on its own it isn't what makes users choose you. So the question becomes whether you keep it internal, where only your own engineers maintain it, or open it up so the whole industry helps make it better. Very often opening it up is the more efficient choice. You get bug reports, contributions, and new use cases you never would have imagined. Graduates come in already knowing your tools, so onboarding is faster. Engineers also like working on things the world can see, so it helps recruiting.

The second layer is about standards and influence. In infrastructure, whoever defines the de facto standard has a lot of say in where the technology goes. When a framework becomes widely used, the hardware vendors, cloud providers, and researchers all start optimizing for it. That gives the company that started it a strong position, even though the code itself is free. From my own experience with frameworks like Caffe and later PyTorch, a lot of the value didn't come from the code. It came from the community and the shared way of thinking that formed around it.

The third layer is that open source is honestly a cultural thing in Silicon Valley. Many of us came from academia, where you publish your work and others build on it. Releasing code is a natural extension of publishing a paper. Companies that respect that culture find it easier to attract strong researchers and engineers.

That said, I don't want to paint it as purely idealistic. Companies are rational. They open-source things that are complementary to their business, not things that are their core moat. And there's a real cost: once you release something, you take on a responsibility to maintain it, handle the community, and keep it stable. Many projects get released and then quietly die because the company didn't invest in that long-term. So the companies that do open source well treat it as a strategic, long-term commitment, not just a PR move or a one-time code dump.

So in short, it's a mix of efficiency, ecosystem strategy, and culture. When those three line up, open source becomes a win-win for the company and for the industry.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the first thing to understand is that open source, for internet companies, is rarely an act of charity. It's a strategic decision, and the economics work out differently than most people assume.

When I was at Berkeley building Caffe, and later at Google and Facebook, I saw this from both sides. For a company like Google, releasing TensorFlow wasn't about giving away the crown jewels. The framework itself isn't the moat. The moat is the data, the infrastructure, the talent, and the ability to run these systems at scale. Open-sourcing the framework actually strengthens those things. It brings the whole research community onto your tools, it makes your engineers more productive because the world is debugging and extending your code, and it means every new graduate already knows your stack when you hire them.

Second, there's a standards argument. If you're building a platform business, you want the ecosystem to converge on your abstractions. Whoever defines the interface that millions of developers use has enormous influence over where the industry goes. Android is the classic example, but PyTorch and TensorFlow follow the same logic. Being open is how you win that convergence, because nobody wants to standardize on something they can't inspect or control.

Third, and this is underappreciated, open source is a talent story. The best engineers want their work to be seen. If you tell a world-class researcher that everything they build stays locked inside the company, you'll lose them to the place that lets them publish and release. Open source is part of the compensation package, in a sense. It's how companies attract and keep people who could work anywhere.

Now, there's a tension here, and I don't want to pretend otherwise. Companies open-source what's complementary to their business and keep closed what's core. Facebook can release PyTorch because Facebook doesn't sell deep learning frameworks. It sells attention. The framework being free makes the whole field move faster, and Facebook benefits from a faster field. But you won't see them open-source the ranking models that run the feed. That's the actual product.

And the dynamics shift over time. In the early days of a technology wave, openness accelerates everyone, and the leaders are confident enough in their lead to share. As things mature and the technology itself becomes the product, you see companies pull back. We're watching that happen right now with large language models. The same organizations that championed open research a few years ago are being much more selective about what they release, because the model weights are now the business.

So my honest view is that open source from internet companies is a kind of enlightened self-interest. It's genuinely good for the world, it has moved the field forward enormously, and I'm a big believer in it. But it works because incentives are aligned, not because of goodwill alone. When you understand which incentives are at play, you can predict pretty well what a company will share and what it won't.

astra-6.text:
I think internet companies support open source because their business model often allows them to benefit from sharing software. If your core business is a search engine, an e-commerce platform, or a social network, you don’t necessarily make money by selling the infrastructure underneath it. You make money by providing a service. So releasing some of that infrastructure can help other developers without giving away everything that makes your business valuable.

And there’s a return. If more people use a project, they can find problems, contribute improvements, and build tools around it. It can also make recruiting easier: developers who already know your technology have a shorter learning curve when they join the company.

But I would distinguish releasing code from sustaining an open-source project. Publishing a repository is relatively easy. Maintaining it, writing documentation, reviewing contributions, and giving people outside the company a meaningful voice require a continuing investment. A company’s willingness to do those things tells you much more about its commitment.

So I don’t see commercial interests and open source as inherently contradictory. The strongest projects are often those where the company’s interests and the community’s needs reinforce each other.

sol-6.1.text:
I think internet companies support open source for a combination of practical and strategic reasons. They depend on a huge amount of open-source infrastructure themselves, so contributing back helps maintain the foundation their businesses run on. And when they release something they’ve built internally, they can attract developers, get feedback, and make that technology better than they could on their own.

The key question is where the company’s competitive advantage actually comes from. If it comes from the product, the service, or how well the company operates, then sharing an underlying software framework doesn’t necessarily weaken that advantage. It may expand the whole ecosystem and make it easier to hire people who already know the tools.

But releasing code is only the beginning. You have to write documentation, review contributions, and give people confidence that the project will continue to be maintained. So I’d judge a company’s commitment less by whether it puts a repository online and more by whether it invests in a community around it.
